- Model tends to overestimate prices in early forecast periods, especially after sharp spikes or volatility.
- Forecast often peaks too early or too high, then underestimates subsequent corrections — suggesting lag in recognizing mean reversion.
- Model underestimates true outcomes in the first 5–10 days after a spike, then gradually catches up — implies delayed reaction to recent high volatility.
- Forecasts show persistent bias toward higher values in the middle of the 30-day window, especially around day 15–20 — may reflect overconfidence in recent trends.
- Model fails to account for downward momentum after a peak — often underestimates the “pullback” phase.
- Forecast tends to be overly optimistic in the first 3–5 days after a new low — may be reacting to recent data too quickly.
- Model exhibits “overshoot” behavior after a spike — forecasts peak higher than true outcome, then corrects — suggests model is not adjusting for volatility decay.
- Mean reversion is not fully captured — model often holds high forecasts for too long after a peak, ignoring the tendency to return to prior levels.
- Forecasts are generally too high in the first 10 days of the 30-day window, then gradually adjust — implies model is not properly weighting recent data or volatility.
- Model underestimates true outcomes in the final 5–10 days of the 30-day window — may be due to insufficient weighting of recent low volatility periods.
